name: Medial canthus cutting

lead: Medial canthus cutting is a term used on looksmaxxing forums for self-made cuts at the inner corner of the eye, aimed at changing how the eye looks, for example making it appear wider or less covered by skin. It echoes real surgeries of the inner eye corner, such as medial canthoplasty and epicanthoplasty, which surgeons perform for both reconstructive and cosmetic reasons.

Published work covers the clinical procedures, not the DIY version: small case series on medial canthoplasty for eyelid disorders and aesthetic Asian eyelid surgery, and veterinary studies. Forum discussion mostly consists of questions about whether it is worthwhile and warnings from other members.

paras: Clinically, medial canthal procedures are carried out by oculoplastic or plastic surgeons with sterile technique and anaesthesia, often alongside other eyelid work. Forum accounts of home attempts exist, but this article does not describe methods.

The inner corner contains the tear drainage canals and small blood vessels. Surgeons report scarring as the main concern after inner-corner procedures, and complication-revision surgery is an established category. Self-performed cuts carry risks of infection, scarring, tear-duct injury and bleeding near the eye, and forum members themselves frequently warn against it.

angle.text: People interested in it hope to change eye shape or reduce the look of eyelid cover at the inner corner. Clinical medial canthoplasty and epicanthoplasty are the surgeon-performed versions of that goal; the DIY form is a forum practice.

lead: Medial canthus cutting is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for altering the medial canthus, the inner corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet, by making an incision. People who discuss it are typically interested in changing eye shape, such as reducing how much of the eyelid or skin covers the inner corner or changing the apparent eye tilt or width. Some forum questions focus on whether it reduces upper eyelid exposure.[1]

The idea borrows from canthoplasty, plastic surgery on the medial or lateral canthus that is described as common in cosmetic procedures and also used to correct eyelid function or position.[2] Related clinical operations include medial epicanthoplasty, which modifies the epicanthic fold of skin that covers the inner corner in many people of East Asian and other ancestries.[3][4]

Published studies deal with clinical procedures: titanium microplate or anchor fixation in blepharophimosis and ectropion, microsurgical work in Asian eyelid surgery, and large veterinary series.[5][6][7][8] No published study tests a do-it-yourself cut. The forum discussion includes both people curious about the idea and others who call it dangerous.
infobox: Eye-corner alteration (forum practice; clinical equivalents exist)

paras: The medial canthus is the point where upper and lower eyelids meet nearest the nose. An epicanthic fold, a vertical skin fold that can cover this corner, occurs with varying frequency across populations and is nearly universal among adults in Japan and South Korea, according to Wikipedia.[4] Four fold types are described: supraciliaris, palpebralis, tarsalis and inversus.[4]
Forum users describe medial canthus cutting as a self-performed version of surgery to open or reshape this area. Threads ask whether it helps with eyelid exposure or is worthwhile.[1][9]

Canthoplasty is plastic surgery on the corners of the eyelids and is separate from canthotomy, a cut made to relieve orbital pressure.[2] Epicanthoplasty modifies epicanthal folds, which sit over the tear drainage canals, and the procedure may leave visible scar lines; Z-plasty is a common technique to address them.[3]
Surgeons also use medial canthoplasty in conditions such as blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome, where eyelid fissures are narrow, and in severe medial ectropion.[5][6][7]

Posts in forum threads state that the inner-corner region has many nerves and vessels and includes the tear system, and that mistakes could harm vision or drainage. Clinical literature describes the same anatomy: the tear drainage canals lie under the epicanthal fold.[3] Scarring is the one complication named in both the surgical and forum material.[3]
Regulators and surgical bodies generally treat such procedures as operations for trained clinicians, and veterinary and human series describe complications even in specialist hands.[8]

Discussion on looksmax.org ranges from curiosity about outcomes to repeated warnings and questions about whether the change is worth the risk.[1][9] Members interested in eye-shape change also discuss clinical options and eyelid exposure.

No studies found on self-performed cutting. Studies of clinical medial canthoplasty include a series of 10 patients with severe medial ectropion treated with bone fixation, reporting good functional and cosmetic results,[6] a report of titanium microplate fixation in children with blepharophimosis,[7] a microsurgical aesthetic Asian double-eyelid method used in 37 patients over six years,[5] and a review of BPES surgery.[10] Veterinary reports include a 601-dog series of a modified medial canthoplasty.[8]
